statement: A report that scores only a bounded artifact — one pinned tree, one revision — can be entirely correct about that artifact and still be misread as a claim about the larger system it belongs to, if the boundary itself never appears on the artifact. A repository whose test suite lives in a separate repository, run by its own CI, is correctly reported as having zero test files against its source files; that statement is true about the tree and false about the system, and a reader holding only the artifact cannot tell which kind of statement they have. The fix is not to hedge the fact (a finding that says evidence was not found stays exactly as stated) — it is to state the scope boundary once, in the reader's own reading path, alongside the fact. Confining a claim to what was examined relocates the evidentiary burden onto the reader noticing the confinement; it does not reduce that burden, and a report that never says where its boundary is increases it.

Before wiring a conditional disclosure line to 'when signal X fires, name the specific cause,' verify a real fixture can actually reach that branch — a classification function that CAN return a specific reason does not mean every code path that produces that reason routes through attribution. In this codebase, a too-large file is recorded as skipped, unattributed, for every tracked file at file-inventory time (before any per-criterion collector runs); only two specific signals, gated to one rubric version, ever re-claim that skip against themselves. A wholesale (whole-criterion) 'too large' abstention bucket built by splitting the existing bundled message looked reasonable from the classification code alone, but was unreachable by any real repository scan — dead code whose prose would have read as a coverage claim the scanner does not actually have. The check that caught it was writing the fixture and watching it fail to trigger, not reading the code that constructs the message.
